topics.title: Fitness, physical activity, exercise and sport

sections.heading: Key definitions
bullets: Physical fitness is the ability to perform ordinary and unexpected daily tasks effectively and safely, without undue fatigue, while retaining energy for leisure and emergencies. Fitness changes over time and differs between people.
Physical activity is bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that uses energy. It includes movement at work, at home, during transport and recreation.
Exercise is a subset of physical activity: it is planned, structured and repetitive movement intended to maintain or improve one or more components of fitness.
Sport is organized, rule-governed and competitive activity. Exercise need not be competitive, and not all physical activity is structured as exercise.
Wellness is broader than fitness and includes multiple dimensions of wellbeing; fitness contributes to a person’s capacity to function and participate in daily life.

sections.heading: Why the distinctions matter
paragraphs: A walk to complete an errand is physical activity; a planned brisk walk repeated on a schedule to improve endurance is exercise; a regulated race is sport. The same movement can fit more than one description depending on its structure and purpose.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define all four terms and give an example that shows how they differ.
Explain why physical fitness is multidimensional and can change over time.
Distinguish general daily movement from a planned training session.

sections.heading: Principles of effective training
bullets: Overload: improvement requires a training demand above the accustomed level, applied safely. The stimulus can be adjusted through frequency, intensity, time or type.
FITT: Frequency is how often; Intensity is how hard; Time is duration; Type is the activity selected. Together these describe a program’s training dose.
Progression: increase demand gradually as the body adapts. Large sudden increases in volume or intensity can contribute to excessive fatigue, loss of motivation or injury.
Specificity: adaptation is specific to the muscles, movements, energy systems and skills trained. Prepare using activities that match the desired outcome.
Rest and recovery allow adaptation between demanding sessions. Periodization organizes training into phases with planned variation in workload and recovery.
Reversibility: adaptations can diminish when training is reduced or stopped; maintaining activity helps retain gains.
Individual differences: age, health, baseline fitness, experience, goals and response to exercise vary, so one program does not suit everyone.

sections.heading: Planning and sustaining activity
bullets: Set a clear, realistic goal and choose activities that fit the person’s interests, schedule, access and current ability.
Begin at a manageable level, monitor how the body responds, and progress one or more FITT variables gradually.
Build consistency through a routine, tracking progress and planning for barriers such as time, weather, cost or low motivation.
Exercise should challenge the body without treating pain as proof of effectiveness. Distinguish expected effort from warning signs that require stopping and reassessment.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Apply FITT to design a simple activity plan for a stated goal.
Explain overload, progression, specificity and reversibility with one example each.
Describe how recovery and individual differences affect a training program.

units.title: Unit 2 - Health Benefits of Physical Activity

sections.heading: Core concepts
paragraphs: Hypokinetic conditions are health problems associated with too little regular movement. The module links physical activity with prevention and management of several chronic conditions, while recognizing that activity is one part of health rather than a guarantee against disease.

sections.heading: Conditions discussed
bullets: Cardiovascular disease, including coronary heart disease and hypertension, concerns the heart and blood vessels. Regular activity can support cardiovascular function and risk-factor management.
Dyslipidemia refers to unhealthy blood lipid patterns, including elevated cholesterol or triglycerides. Activity, nutrition and other health factors can influence risk.
Diabetes mellitus involves problems with blood glucose regulation. Physical activity supports glucose use by working muscles and is an important part of broader health management.
Overweight and obesity involve excess body fat that can affect health. Energy balance, activity, food intake, genetics and social conditions can all be relevant.
Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risk factors rather than one isolated disease; the module discusses its connection to inactivity and cardiovascular risk.
Ageing is associated with changes in physical capacity. Regular appropriate activity can help maintain function, mobility and independence.
Musculoskeletal disorders and postural problems can affect movement and comfort. Strength, mobility and balanced movement habits can support function; causes and suitable responses vary.

sections.heading: Activity, risk and responsible interpretation
bullets: Physical activity can improve health-related risk factors, but individual outcomes depend on many influences, including existing conditions and environment.
Different forms of activity stress the body differently; choose activities suitable to personal capacity and goals.
Avoid turning population-level associations into guarantees about one person. Health claims should be stated proportionately and interpreted with context.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define hypokinetic condition and explain how inactivity can relate to chronic disease risk.
Name several conditions covered in the unit and connect each to a plausible benefit of regular activity.
Explain why activity is important but should not be presented as the only determinant of health.

topics.title: Nutrition, food energy and sound eating practices

sections.heading: Nutrients and their roles
bullets: Macronutrients are needed in comparatively large amounts: carbohydrates, fats and proteins. They provide energy and materials for body functions, growth and repair.
Carbohydrates are a major energy source; proteins provide amino acids for building and maintaining tissues; fats provide concentrated energy and serve structural and regulatory roles.
Micronutrients include vitamins and minerals. They do not provide energy directly but are needed for normal processes such as metabolism, tissue function and fluid balance.
Water is essential for transport, temperature regulation and normal body processes. Needs vary with activity, environment and individual factors.

sections.heading: Calories and energy balance
bullets: A calorie (food Calorie, commonly written kcal) is a unit of energy. Food energy is primarily supplied by carbohydrate, protein and fat.
Energy balance compares energy intake with energy expenditure over time. It influences body mass but does not alone describe diet quality or overall health.
A well-informed eating pattern considers variety, nutrient density, portions, availability and personal needs rather than focusing on a single food or nutrient.
The module’s recommendations should be understood in their course context; needs differ by age, activity, health status and other circumstances.

sections.heading: Food choices and performance
bullets: A training diet should provide sufficient energy and nutrients to support daily activity, recovery and adaptation.
Before exercise, food choices and timing can affect comfort and energy availability. Allow enough time for digestion and consider the activity’s duration and intensity.
During prolonged or demanding activity, fluid and energy needs may rise. Appropriate intake depends on exercise conditions and individual requirements.
After exercise, eating and drinking help replace energy and fluid and support recovery. A balanced meal or snack can combine carbohydrate, protein and fluids as appropriate.
Plan meals around training demands and ordinary routines; avoid assuming one rigid timing plan works for everyone.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish macronutrients from micronutrients and state a function of each group.
Explain calorie and energy balance while noting why energy alone does not measure diet quality.
Compare nutrition considerations before, during and after exercise.

units.title: Unit 4 - Health-Related Fitness and Exercise Prescription

sections.heading: Cardiorespiratory fitness
paragraphs: Cardiorespiratory fitness describes the capacity of the circulatory and respiratory systems to supply oxygen during sustained activity. It is developed through regular aerobic activities such as brisk walking, running, cycling, swimming or dancing, with intensity matched to the person’s level.

sections.heading: Muscle fitness
bullets: Muscular strength is the capacity to exert force against resistance. Muscular endurance is the capacity to sustain or repeat contractions over time.
Resistance training can use body weight, free weights, machines, bands or other resistance. Load, repetitions, sets, rest and movement technique affect the training stimulus.
Balanced training should address major muscle groups and use controlled technique, appropriate resistance and recovery.

sections.heading: Flexibility and body composition
bullets: Flexibility is the range of motion available at a joint or group of joints. It is influenced by muscles, connective tissues, joint structure, temperature and activity habits.
Flexibility exercises should be controlled and suited to the target area. Avoid bouncing or forcing a joint beyond a comfortable range.
Body composition describes the relative amounts of fat mass and fat-free components such as muscle, bone and body water. It is distinct from body weight alone.
No single field measure captures every aspect of body composition perfectly; interpretation depends on method, measurement conditions and limitations.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: List the four health-related fitness components and define each.
Distinguish muscular strength from muscular endurance with examples.
Explain why body composition is different from total body mass.

topics.title: Exercise prescription, workout structure and safety

sections.heading: Building an exercise prescription
bullets: Start with a goal and consider baseline fitness, health status, preferences, available equipment and schedule.
Use FITT to describe the plan: how often, how hard, how long and what type of activity.
Choose mode of exercise that matches the goal and applies the desired stimulus. Specificity matters: training for a particular event should include relevant practice.
Individualize and progress the plan gradually. Monitor response and allow recovery rather than increasing every variable at once.

sections.heading: Workout phases
bullets: Warm-up: a gradual transition that prepares the body for the main activity, often beginning with light movement and progressing toward the session’s demands.
Primary conditioning period: the main workout, where the planned aerobic, strength, endurance or flexibility stimulus is applied.
Cool-down: a gradual reduction in activity that allows the body to transition toward resting conditions; it can include light movement and appropriate flexibility work.
A session should be organized so that technique and safety are maintained as fatigue develops.

sections.heading: Developing cardiorespiratory fitness
bullets: Select a sustained or interval activity that recruits large muscle groups and can be performed consistently.
Set frequency, intensity and duration in line with current capacity; progress workload in manageable steps.
Use perceived effort, the talk test, heart-rate information where appropriate, or other methods taught in the module to monitor intensity.
Starting and maintaining a program depends on realistic goals, enjoyable activities, routine, gradual progression and ways to track adherence.

sections.heading: Safety and avoiding hazardous exercise
bullets: Use appropriate equipment, environment, technique and hydration practices. Adjust activity for heat, cold, terrain and other conditions.
Avoid excessive increases in training load and allow rest. Fatigue can reduce coordination and increase the chance of poor technique.
Recognize that health conditions, medications and individual circumstances can change what exercise is suitable; use appropriate professional guidance where needed.
The module emphasizes sensible exercise habits rather than ‘no pain, no gain’: discomfort is not a required sign of benefit.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Describe the role of warm-up, conditioning and cool-down in a workout.
Use FITT to outline a progressive cardiorespiratory program for a hypothetical beginner.
Identify risk factors in an unsafe exercise plan and propose practical adjustments.

sections.heading: Why assess fitness
paragraphs: Fitness assessment provides information about current status and can help set goals, monitor change and evaluate a program. Results are estimates under specific test conditions, not a complete diagnosis of health or ability.

sections.heading: Good testing practice
bullets: Choose a test that measures the intended component and is appropriate for the participant’s ability and circumstances.
Use standardized instructions, equipment, warm-up, timing and recording so results can be compared fairly.
Explain the procedure, obtain cooperation, record units correctly and apply the same protocol when reassessing.
Safety comes first: consider readiness and stop a test if concerning symptoms arise. A field test should not be treated as a substitute for clinical evaluation.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Explain why a fitness test result is not the same as a medical diagnosis.
Name factors that improve consistency and fairness in testing.
Match the assessment to the component it is intended to measure.

topics.title: Tests for cardiorespiratory, muscle, flexibility and body composition

sections.heading: Cardiorespiratory fitness tests
bullets: The 1.5-mile run test estimates cardiorespiratory capacity from the time required to cover a set distance; performance is influenced by pacing, motivation and running familiarity.
The 1-mile walk test uses walking time and physiological response measures as specified by the protocol. Follow the required pace and measurement procedure.
Cycle ergometer tests use work rate and physiological response during cycling; workload increments and stopping criteria must follow the test protocol.
Step tests use stepping at a set height and cadence, often evaluating recovery response. Step height, duration and pulse measurement timing affect results.
These field or submaximal methods estimate fitness; they do not directly measure every aspect of aerobic capacity and should be interpreted according to their protocol.

sections.heading: Muscle fitness and flexibility tests
bullets: Muscular strength assessments measure the greatest force or load produced under a defined procedure. The test should specify movement, equipment and whether the attempt is maximal or estimated.
Muscular endurance assessments count repeated contractions or time a sustained position using consistent range and technique.
Trunk flexibility can be assessed with a standardized reach test; shoulder flexibility uses a movement or reach protocol to assess range. Results are specific to the tested motion and technique.
Warm-up and consistent instructions matter; comparisons are meaningful only when protocol and conditions are similar.

sections.heading: Body composition assessment
bullets: Skinfold testing estimates subcutaneous fat at specified sites using calipers and a standard procedure. Site location, measurer skill and prediction equations influence the estimate.
Other field techniques may estimate body composition from circumference, body mass index or other measures. Each method has assumptions and limitations.
Body mass index relates mass to height squared but does not directly distinguish fat mass from lean mass; interpret it as a screening measure rather than a direct body-composition measurement.
Use the method consistently for tracking and avoid treating small changes as meaningful when measurement error could explain them.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Match each named field test to the fitness component it assesses and explain the basic measurement used.
State at least one limitation for each assessment method.
Explain how standardization, safety and consistent retesting improve the usefulness of fitness data.
